passages.title: A Debate to Remember
passages.text:
Last week I watched a televised debate between two candidates for mayor. The first **politician**, a retired teacher, gave a calm and **sensible** answer about road safety. His opponent, however, started making **silly** jokes and called his rival's plan "stupid". Some viewers thought it was funny, but I found it embarrassing.

The debate was also **confusing**. Both speakers kept changing the numbers, and the presenter's questions did not help either. I felt **confused**, and so did my sister, who was sitting next to me. "Why do they **confuse** us on purpose?" she asked. I think some people hope that voters will not check the facts.

Near the end, the older candidate talked about his father, and his voice shook. It is natural to **get emotional** when you talk about family, and I respected him for being honest. My sister, who is a very **emotional** person, even cried a little. In the end, I voted for him because he seemed more thoughtful than his rival.

passages.title: Lan and the Radio
passages.text:
My cousin Lan was a **curious** child. She asked questions about everything: why the sky is blue, where rain comes from, how the neighbour's radio works. Her **curiosity** sometimes got her into trouble, like the day she took the radio apart. My aunt found her sitting among wires, **curiously** studying a small green circuit board.

I was **jealous** of her in those days. At school, teachers praised her, and I used to watch her **jealously** from the back of the class. Looking back, my **jealousy** was pointless, because she never tried to compete with me. She simply loved learning.

Last year I visited her in Da Nang. I expected her to be tired after a hard year at university, but she was as **cheerful** as ever, laughing and singing in the kitchen. I, on the other hand, felt **miserable** because I had failed a driving test that week. Lan listened to me, made tea, and reminded me that one bad day does not define a person. Her kindness made me feel much better.

passages.title: When the Mind Needs Care
passages.text:
According to a recent health report, nearly one in five young adults will **suffer from** one of the many **mental disorders** at least once in their lives. The term covers a wide range of problems. People with **anxiety disorders**, for example, may feel afraid or worried for no clear reason, while those with **sleep disorders** cannot rest properly at night. **Eating disorders** are also common among teenagers who feel strong pressure about their appearance.

Doctors explain that a **disorder** is not the same as a bad mood. It is a medical condition that affects how a person thinks and behaves every day. **Depression** is one of the best-known examples. Someone with **depression** may feel **depressed** for weeks, lose interest in hobbies, and see everything as **depressing**, even good news.

The report urges families to take these signs seriously. Talking early, it says, makes treatment much easier. It also recommends that schools provide counselling, so that students do not have to face their problems alone.

passages.title: Exam Day Nerves
passages.text:
Every summer, thousands of Vietnamese students **take an exam** to enter university. In Britain, students usually **do an exam** called the A-level instead. The idea is the same: each **candidate** sits in a quiet hall and answers questions for two or three hours, while teachers walk around to make sure nobody cheats.

My friend Minh was always **frightened of** that day. He worried that he would forget everything he had learned and would **fail an exam** that decided his future. His parents told him that failure was not the end of the world. If he did not **pass an exam**, he could simply **retake an exam** the following year.

Minh felt calmer after that conversation. He studied steadily, slept well, and arrived at the hall early. When the results came out in July, he had passed with a score high enough for his first-choice school. He still says the waiting was the hardest part.

passages.title: A Plan for Revision
passages.text:
Three weeks before her final exams, Hoa made a plan. She decided to **revise for** each subject at a fixed time, starting at seven every morning. She would **do some revision** in the library, then go for a short walk. In her notebook she wrote: Maths on Monday, History on Tuesday.

Hoa's older brother thought her timetable was too strict. "It will **depress** you," he said. "You'll have no fun." But Hoa knew that good **exam preparation** is about balance. She would **do exam preparation** in short blocks of forty minutes and then rest. Each block ended with a quick **revision** of the key points, which helped her remember them.

On the morning of the first test, Hoa felt ready. She walked **energetically** through the school gate, smiling at her classmates. Her brother was wrong: the plan did not make her unhappy at all. It simply gave her confidence.

passages.title: The Speech Mr Harris Gives
passages.text:
At the start of every term, Mr Harris, our English teacher, gives the same speech. "Some of you will **do well** in this course," he says, "and some will **do badly**. The difference is rarely intelligence. It is effort."

He tells us that nobody expects perfection. "All I ask is that you **do your best**," he says. "If you **try your best** every day, you will improve, even when it feels slow."

Mr Harris is also honest about results. In British schools you **get a good mark** by answering clearly and giving examples, and in many American schools you **get a good grade** by doing the same thing. Whatever word you use, a **grade** is only a small piece of information. It tells you what happened on one test, not who you are.

I used to ignore this speech. Now I understand it, because last year I improved from a C to a B simply by working steadily.

passages.title: Learning to Write an Essay
passages.text:
Writing has never been easy for me. I **find it difficult to** organise my ideas, and my first drafts are usually a mess. When my tutor asked us to **do an essay** on city life, I almost panicked.

I decided to **work on** one skill at a time. First, I wrote a plan with three main points. Then I wrote one paragraph a day, instead of trying to **get through** the whole essay on the last night. It was slow, and honestly it was **hard work**, but I could see progress.

When the tutor returned the essays, I looked for the **mark** at the bottom of the page. It was 7 out of 10, my best result so far. "**With a bit of luck**, you could reach eight next time," she wrote beside it. I smiled. I knew luck would be only a small part of it; the real reason for my improvement was patience and daily practice.

passages.title: Money in London
passages.text:
When Linh arrived in London for her master's course, the first thing she needed was local money. The **currency** in the United Kingdom is the pound, often called **sterling** in banks and on the news. Her host family showed her the different forms of money. A paper **note** can be worth five, ten, twenty or fifty pounds, while a metal **coin** is worth less, from one penny to two pounds.

To get cash, Linh looked for a **cashpoint** near her flat. Americans would call it **a cash machine**, but British people prefer the first word. She used her new debit card to **take out money** for the week, and the machine printed a receipt showing her balance.

Linh had a clear goal for her first year. She wanted to **be in credit** at the end of every month, which meant never spending more than she had. It was not easy in an expensive city, but she kept a notebook and checked it every Sunday evening.

passages.title: Paying for University
passages.text:
Going to university can be expensive, so many students apply for a **student loan**. In some countries it is easy to **get a loan** from the government, but you must understand the conditions first. The loan usually helps you **pay your fees** and buy books, but it does not cover everything.

A common mistake is to **owe someone money** and forget about it. If you **borrow** a laptop from a friend, for example, return it on time. If you ask a relative to **lend** you some cash, write down the date and the **amount of money**. Clear records protect friendships.

Eventually you will need to **pay back money** that you owe, either to the bank or to people you know. The sooner you start, the smaller the total cost, because interest grows every month. Financial experts also advise students to keep a simple notebook: income on one page, spending on the other. It sounds boring, but it works.

passages.title: My First Flat
passages.text:
I recently started my first job in Ho Chi Minh City, and I am learning how expensive independence is. At the moment I **can't afford** a flat alone, so I share one with two colleagues. We **pay rent** on the first day of each month, and my share is cheap but not tiny.

Before moving in, we had to **pay a deposit** equal to **one month's rent**. The landlord promised to return it when we leave, as long as nothing is broken. To find the money, I decided to **save up for** it by cooking at home and walking to work.

Shopping has become a game, too. Supermarkets often offer **three for the price of two** on shampoo or noodles, and I always take advantage of that deal. My aunt, who is good with money, suggested putting my extra savings into a **certificate of deposit** at her bank. It pays higher interest than a normal account, but I cannot touch the money for a year. For now, I am keeping things simple.

passages.title: A Missed Deadline
passages.text:
On Monday afternoon, our team had a **tense meeting** about a missed deadline. Our manager, Ms Pham, was already angry when she walked in. When Duc admitted that he had forgotten to send the report, she **raised her voice at** him in front of everybody.

Duc replied that sending reports was not in his **job description**, and the argument became worse. Later, Ms Pham admitted that she had spoken **in the heat of the moment**. She said she had been under pressure from the director and had not meant to shout.

The next morning, she told the team that shouting is unacceptable, and that she would not do it again. Then she turned to Duc: "This is the **absolute last time** I will accept a missed deadline." Duc nodded. Both agreed to move on **as long as it doesn't happen again**. The atmosphere in the office slowly improved, and by Friday people were joking in the kitchen again.

passages.title: Talking Like Adults
passages.text:
After the argument, Duc thought carefully about what to do. He felt hurt that Ms Pham had shouted **in front of people**, but he also knew that he had answered rudely. A friend advised him that the best way to **address** a manager about a conflict is to speak first and listen carefully afterwards. So Duc asked for a **one-on-one** meeting in her office.

At first, Ms Pham looked surprised. Then she smiled and said, "Let's **have a conversation like adults**." She listened to his complaints without interrupting, and he did the same when it was her turn. Duc then decided to **apologize for** his behavior, because he had been rude about his job. Ms Pham thanked him and added that she felt ashamed of her own tone.

When Duc left her office, he felt lighter. Both of them were **mature enough to** admit their mistakes, and that, he realised, was the most important step. A conflict at work does not have to damage a relationship if people deal with it calmly and privately.

passages.title: Art Class Basics
passages.text:
In today's art and design class, Ms Green asked each of us to bring a few basic tools. I brought a pencil case with a **rubber**, a plastic **ruler**, and a yellow **highlighter pen**.

First, we drew a rectangle on a sheet of paper. We had to **measure** each side carefully and write the numbers beside it. When Ben made a mistake, he used his **rubber** to **rub out** the wrong line. Then we used the **highlighter pen** to **highlight** the most important dimensions in our notes.

After that, Ms Green showed us how to build a small lamp. She held up the **plug** at the end of the cable and explained that it must always match the **socket** on the wall. "Never touch a **plug** with wet hands," she warned. Later she checked every **socket** in the room before we tried the lamp. We listened carefully and wrote down her safety rules in our notebooks.

passages.title: Making a Safety Film
passages.text:
Our class made a short film about road safety, and my **partner**, Quan, and I were responsible for the sound. On the first day we forgot to bring a speaker, so I asked a classmate, "Could you **lend me** yours?" She said yes, and she even promised to **lend it to** us for the whole week. Quan and I agreed to **share** the cost of new batteries.

We also had to **borrow** a camera from our teacher, because ours was broken. After lunch, we went to the school yard, and I had to **plug in** the speaker so that the actors could hear the music. At first it was too quiet, so I tried to **turn up** the volume. A moment later it was far too loud, and Quan ran over to **turn down** the sound before it hurt anyone's ears.

In the final scene, a cyclist has to **brake hard** to avoid a car. We filmed it five times, because the bike kept sliding on the wet ground. By the end of the day we were tired, but proud of our work.

passages.title: My First English Class
passages.text:
On my first day in an English course, I was too nervous to speak. The teacher, Ms Lee, told us to **work with a partner**, and I was paired with a boy from Brazil. At first we only smiled at each other. Then he asked me, "**How do you pronounce** this word?" I did not know either, so we asked Ms Lee. She said it slowly and asked us to **repeat** it after her.

Over the next weeks, I learned some useful questions. When I did not understand a new word, I asked, "**What does it mean**?" When I was not sure about writing, I asked, "**How do you spell** it?" If I could not see how to apply a word in a sentence, I asked, "**How do you use the word** 'actually'?"

Ms Lee was happy to **correct my English** whenever I wrote something wrong, and she never made me feel ashamed. One afternoon she even taught us to **explain the difference between** 'lend' and 'borrow'. That lesson helped me more than any textbook.
